promptText: What is the Virtual DOM actually made of, and why is 'the VDOM is faster than the real DOM' considered a misconception?
options: It is a tree of plain JavaScript objects; the real win is a declarative model plus batched, minimal DOM mutations, not raw speed of the objects themselves
It is a compiled, low-level shadow copy of the DOM maintained by the browser engine in C++, which is inherently faster to mutate
It is a cache of previously rendered HTML strings that React replays instead of re-parsing markup
It is a WebAssembly module that intercepts DOM writes and executes them off the main thread
explanation: React elements are just plain JS objects created via createElement/jsx(); they are cheap to create and compare in memory, but direct DOM writes are not inherently slow. React's real advantage is computing a minimal, coordinated set of DOM operations rather than the VDOM being intrinsically faster than the DOM.

promptText: React's reconciliation diff is O(n) instead of the theoretically correct O(n^3) for general tree diffing because it relies on two heuristics. What are they?
options: Elements of different types always produce different trees (full teardown), and developers can hint stable identity across renders using keys
React sorts all elements alphabetically by type before comparing them, and ignores props entirely during the first pass
React only ever compares the root node of each tree and assumes all children are unchanged unless told otherwise
React converts both trees into strings and does a character-level diff, which is faster than object comparison
explanation: The two assumptions -- different element types imply different subtrees, and keys give children a stable identity independent of position -- let React approximate the diff in linear time instead of running a full, prohibitively expensive tree-edit-distance algorithm.

promptText: A list of rows uses `key={index}`. When a new item is prepended to the front of the list, what typically goes wrong?
options: Every existing row's key shifts by one position, so React reuses each old fiber/DOM node for a different logical item, and that item's internal state (focus, input value) appears attached to the wrong row
React throws a runtime error immediately because index keys are not permitted for lists longer than one item
Nothing goes wrong; index keys behave identically to stable ID keys as long as the list length does not change
React silently re-mounts the entire list including the container element on every keystroke
explanation: Because reconciliation matches old and new children by key, and index-based keys tie identity to position, inserting at the front shifts every subsequent index so React reuses fibers for the wrong logical items, corrupting per-row state like focus or an in-progress edit.

promptText: A component renders `loggedIn ? <Dashboard /> : <LoginForm />`, and both components happen to internally render a visually identical `<div className="card">`. What does React do when `loggedIn` toggles?
options: It fully unmounts the old component's subtree (destroying its state and DOM) and mounts the new one from scratch, because it compares element type/key, not rendered visual shape
It notices both render a similar div and patches only the differing attributes, preserving both components' internal state
It keeps the DOM node but swaps only the event handlers attached to it
It throws a development warning requiring the two branches to return the same component type
explanation: Reconciliation never inspects what a component's render output looks like -- it only checks the type/key of the element at that slot. Since Dashboard and LoginForm are different function references, React tears down the old subtree entirely and mounts the new one, regardless of visual similarity.

promptText: What was the core limitation of the pre-Fiber 'stack reconciler' that led React to redesign its internals in React 16?
options: It processed the whole tree in one deep, synchronous recursive pass that could not be paused, so a large update could block the main thread and drop frames
It could not support class components, only function components
It required every component to be wrapped in React.memo to render at all
It stored the entire element tree in localStorage between renders, which was slow on large apps
explanation: The stack reconciler relied on native recursion, so once a render started there was no way to yield control back to the browser mid-tree; Fiber turned this into an iterative walk over linked fiber nodes so work could be paused and resumed.

promptText: Why must the render phase (calling component functions) be free of side effects like network calls or ref mutations?
options: Because React may call a component's render function more than once per committed update (e.g. Strict Mode double-invokes it, or a render can be restarted/discarded), so side effects could run multiple times or against a tree that never commits
Because side effects are syntactically disallowed inside JSX and will cause a compile error
Because the render phase runs on a Web Worker where DOM and network APIs are unavailable
Because side effects executed during render are automatically deferred until the component unmounts
explanation: Render-phase work is speculative -- it can be interrupted, restarted, or thrown away, and Strict Mode deliberately double-invokes it in development to surface impurities. A side effect placed there can fire extra times or against a discarded tree, which is why effects belong in useEffect/useLayoutEffect instead.

promptText: Hooks are stored on a fiber as a singly linked list built during render, identified purely by call order rather than by name. What is the direct consequence of this design?
options: Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level every render, because a conditional or looped hook call shifts every subsequent hook's position in the list, causing React to read the wrong state/queue for the wrong hook
Hooks can be called conditionally as long as they are all declared with unique variable names
Custom hooks get their own isolated hooks list, separate from the component that calls them, so ordering inside a custom hook doesn't matter
The order only matters for useState, not for useEffect or useRef, since those use a separate list
explanation: Because React identifies a hook by its position in the linked list rather than by name, skipping a hook call on some renders shifts the cursor for every hook after it, corrupting state -- this is the mechanical reason behind the Rules of Hooks, and it applies transitively through custom hooks since they share the same list.

promptText: Before React 18, calling two setState updates inside a Promise's `.then()` callback caused two separate re-renders. What changed with React 18's automatic batching, and what is required to get it?
options: With `createRoot`, React batches updates from any context -- event handlers, promises, timeouts, native listeners -- into a single render; apps still on legacy `ReactDOM.render` do not get this behavior
React 18 batches updates everywhere automatically regardless of which root API mounted the app, with no opt-in required
Automatic batching only applies inside promises and timeouts, but native event listeners remain unbatched even under createRoot
Batching was removed in React 18 in favor of always flushing each setState synchronously for predictability
explanation: React 18 extends batching to all contexts, but only for roots created with createRoot; an app still using the legacy ReactDOM.render API keeps the old behavior where only updates inside React event handlers were batched.

promptText: React's concurrent scheduler replaced an earlier 'expiration time' priority model with 'lanes' (a 31-bit bitmask). What specific capability does the bitmask add that a single deadline number could not?
options: A fiber can track multiple simultaneously pending priorities as a set and combine/query them with cheap bitwise operations, rather than only being able to express a single ordering via one deadline
Bitmasks allow React to skip the render phase entirely for high-priority updates
Lanes let React run multiple renders on separate OS threads simultaneously
The bitmask replaced React's need for the virtual DOM entirely, diffing lanes directly instead of elements
explanation: A single expiration timestamp can only express ordering ('this vs that'), whereas a bitmask supports true set operations -- a fiber can have multiple distinct pending priorities (e.g. an urgent update and a transition) tracked and combined independently via bitwise OR/AND.

promptText: A component is wrapped in `React.memo`, and its parent re-renders because of unrelated state. The component also consumes a Context whose Provider value just changed. What happens to the memoized component?
options: It re-renders anyway -- Context propagation walks down from the Provider and marks every consumer for update, bypassing the normal bailout that React.memo relies on
React.memo prevents the re-render entirely, since Context changes are subject to the same shallow prop comparison as regular props
It re-renders only if the parent also happens to pass new props, never due to Context alone
React throws a runtime error because memo and Context cannot be used together on the same component
explanation: Context propagation is a special traversal that finds every consumer of a changed context and forces an update on it, deliberately bypassing the bailout mechanisms (including React.memo) that would otherwise skip unaffected subtrees -- this is exactly why an unstable or coarse-grained context value re-renders its whole consumer set.

promptText: A tooltip component measures its own size and repositions itself based on that measurement. Using `useEffect` for this causes a visible one-frame flash in the wrong position; switching to `useLayoutEffect` fixes it. Why?
options: useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before the browser paints, so the repositioning is applied before the user ever sees the frame; useEffect runs asynchronously after paint, so the wrong position is visible first
useEffect only runs on the client while useLayoutEffect runs on both server and client, which explains the flash during hydration
useLayoutEffect has access to updated props one render earlier than useEffect does
useEffect batches its callback across multiple components, delaying execution by an arbitrary number of frames
explanation: useLayoutEffect fires in the commit phase's layout sub-phase, synchronously, before the browser paints -- ideal for measure-then-adjust patterns. useEffect is a passive effect deferred until after paint, so any visual correction it makes is visible to the user one frame late.

promptText: A team replaces a 300ms debounce on a search filter with `startTransition`, expecting identical behavior, but is surprised the expensive filter function still runs on every keystroke. What is the actual distinction between the two?
options: A debounce delays WHEN the function is called at all (via a timer); a transition calls the function immediately every time but only deprioritizes WHEN the resulting render is reflected on screen, so it does not reduce how often the work runs
startTransition and debounce are functionally identical; the observed behavior must be a bug in the transition implementation
startTransition cancels all but the last keystroke's update automatically, exactly like a debounce, but with zero configurable delay
Debounce only works with class components, so the migration to startTransition should have also converted the component to a class
explanation: startTransition marks an update's render as low priority and interruptible but dispatches it synchronously and immediately, so the expensive computation still runs every time it's called; a debounce genuinely delays invocation itself via a timer, reducing the number of times the work runs.

options: Defining Inner inside Outer's body creates a brand-new function reference on every render of Outer; since reconciliation reuses a fiber only when both key AND type match by reference, React sees a 'different type' each time and fully remounts Inner, wiping its state
useState resets automatically whenever it is declared inside a nested function component rather than a top-level one
React caches components by name string, and two functions both named 'Inner' across renders collide and force a reset
The button's onClick handler closes over a stale n, which forces React to unmount and remount the whole subtree to refresh the closure
explanation: Reconciliation's reuse rule requires the element's type to be referentially identical across renders. Defining Inner inside Outer creates a new function object every render, so type equality fails every time, triggering the same full teardown/rebuild as any other type-mismatch case -- a closures/scope bug wearing a reconciliation costume.

promptText: After a component has been updated many times (well past its first mount and first update), how many fiber objects does React typically keep allocated for that single component position, and why?
options: Exactly two -- the current and work-in-progress fibers keep swapping roles via the `alternate` pointer, so after the one-time allocation on the first update, subsequent renders only patch the existing pair instead of allocating new objects
One per render that ever occurred, since each fiber is kept for potential rollback and garbage collected only when the app unmounts entirely
Zero once the component stabilizes, since React converts stable components into static DOM nodes with no fiber backing
A new fiber every render, but they are pooled and reused across different, unrelated components to reduce allocation
explanation: createWorkInProgress only allocates a second fiber once, on the render immediately following mount, wiring it as the first fiber's alternate; every later render just reuses whichever of the two objects is not currently 'current', patching its fields -- a deliberate memory-reuse optimization on top of the double-buffering correctness guarantee.

promptText: Suspense-for-data-fetching (throwing a promise during render, showing a fallback, retrying later) could not have been built on React's old stack reconciler. Which specific Fiber capability does it fundamentally depend on?
options: The ability to safely abandon a partially-completed work-in-progress tree (via double buffering) without corrupting the visible current tree, and later resume/retry rendering that subtree from an ordinary scheduled update once a 'ping' fires
The ability to run multiple component render functions in parallel on separate threads while waiting for a promise to resolve
The ability to serialize the entire fiber tree to JSON and rehydrate it later, which the stack reconciler's call stack could not do
The addition of async/await syntax to component function bodies, which the stack reconciler's transpiler did not support
explanation: Suspense needs to stop mid-subtree, substitute fallback content for just that boundary, and retry an arbitrary time later without corrupting anything already on screen. This maps directly onto Fiber's double-buffered current/work-in-progress trees (safe abandonment) and the ping-based retry going through the normal scheduling entry point -- neither of which the recursive, run-to-completion stack reconciler could support, since it had no persisted, resumable representation of 'where rendering was' independent of the native call stack.
